title.en: The Transformations of the Dead: Hawk, Lotus, Benu, Swallow, and Crocodile
title.zh: 亡者之變形：鷹、蓮、貝努、燕與鱷

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (Book of the Dead, chapters of taking forms)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（亡靈書變形諸章）

texts.period: Book of the Dead chs. 76-89, Theban recension c. 1550-1292 BCE (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the summary of the transformation chapters

summary.en: The shapeshifter's catalogue of the Book of the Dead: chapters 76-89 enable the dead to transform into the Light-god, the primeval soul of God, Ptah, Osiris, a golden hawk, a divine hawk, a lotus, a benu bird, a heron, a swallow, a serpent, and a crocodile — 'and into any being or thing he pleased' — while ch. 89 lets the soul rejoin its body at pleasure.
summary.zh: 亡靈書之變形目錄：第七六至八九章使亡者能化為光神、太初神魂、卜塔、奧西里斯、金鷹、神鷹、蓮花、貝努鳥、蒼鷺、燕、蛇與鱷——『且能化為任何存在或之物』；第八九章更使魂可隨意歸返其身。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary chapters summarized in Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Chaps. 76-89 enabled a man to transform himself into the Light-god, the primeval soul of God, the gods Ptah and Osiris, a golden hawk, a divine hawk, a lotus, a benu bird, a heron, a swallow, a serpent, a crocodile, and into any being or thing he pleased. Chap. 89 enabled the soul of the deceased to rejoin its body at pleasure, and Chaps. 91 and 92 secured the egress of his soul and spirit from the tomb.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, summary of the Book of the Dead chapters.

title.en: The Souls of Pe and Nekhen: Knowing the Gods of the Cities
title.zh: 布托與奈肯之魂：識城之神

region.en: Pe (Buto) and Nekhen, Egypt (the pre-dynastic capitals and their souls)
region.zh: 埃及布托（佩）與奈肯（前王朝故都及其神魂）

texts.period: Book of the Dead chs. 108-119, Theban recension (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the chapters on the Souls of the towns

summary.en: Before the dead may sail the skies he must know the souls of the ancient cities: chapters 108-119 enable him 'to know the Souls of the East and West, and of the towns of Pe (Buto), Nekhen, Khemenu (Hermopolis), and Anu (Heliopolis)' — the divine inhabitants of Egypt's oldest shrines, the predynastic souls whose company admits the newcomer.
summary.zh: 亡者欲航於天，必先識古城之魂：第一〇八至一一九章使其『得知東西之魂，及布托、奈肯、赫爾莫波利斯與赫利奧波利斯諸城之魂』——埃及最古聖地之神居，知其名者方得同行。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary chapters summarized in Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Chaps. 108, 109, 112, and 116 enabled him to know the Souls (i.e. gods) of the East and West, and of the towns of Pe, Nekhen, Khemenu, and Anu. Chaps. 117-119 enabled him to find his way through Rastau, a part of the kingdom of Seker, the god of Death.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, summary.

title.en: Herfhaf the Ferryman: None but the Righteous May Land
title.zh: 渡者赫爾哈夫：唯義者得登岸

region.en: The celestial river of the Egyptian Other World (symbolic pin, Abydos region)
region.zh: 埃及冥界天河（象徵定位，阿拜多斯一帶）

texts.period: Book of the Dead chs. 98-99 and 125, Theban recension (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the celestial ferryman

summary.en: The ferryman of the dead: chapters 98-99 secure the use of the magical boat and the services of the celestial ferryman, who ferries the justified across the river of the Tuat to the Island of Fire where Osiris lives — and none but the righteous may enter his boat, none but the righteous land on the island; at the Great Judgment the deceased declares 'I have testified before Herfhaf, and he hath approved me.'
summary.zh: 亡者之渡者：第九八至九九章使亡者得用魔法之舟，由天渡者載其渡冥界之河至奧西里斯所居之火島——唯義者得登其舟、得履其島；大審判時亡者自陳：『我已陳於赫爾哈夫之前，而彼許我。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary chapters via Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Chaps. 98 and 99 secured for him the use of the magical boat, and the services of the celestial ferryman, who would ferry him across the river in the Tuat to the Island of Fire, in which Osiris lived. Chaps. 101 and 102 provided access for him to the Boat of Ra.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, summary.

passages.text: I have testified before Herfhaf, and he hath approved me. I have seen the things over which the Persea tree spreadeth [its branches] in Rastau. I offer up my prayers to the gods, and I know their persons. I have come and have advanced to declare the truth and to set up the Balance on its stand in Aukert.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. IV, from Book of the Dead ch. 125 (Herfhaf = the celestial ferryman; footnote: 'None but the righteous could enter his boat, and none but the righteous was allowed to land on the Island of Osiris').

title.en: The Ship of Osiris and the Argo: Canopus the Pilot
title.zh: 奧西里斯之舟與阿爾戈號：舵師卡諾普斯

region.en: The night sky between Orion and the Dog Star (constellation of the ship of Osiris)
region.zh: 獵戶座與天狼星之間的夜空（奧西里斯舟之星座）

texts.period: Recorded by Plutarch, De Iside 22 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XXII

summary.en: The euhemerist reading of the gods, from Plutarch's Egyptian priests: Hermes had one hand shorter than the other, Typhon was red-complexioned, Horus fair, Osiris black — men subject to human accidents; Osiris was a general, Canopus (the star) a pilot, 'and the ship which the Greeks call Argo, being made in imitation of the ship of Osiris, was, in honour of him, turned into a constellation and placed near Orion and the Dog-star, the former being sacred to Horus and the latter to Isis.'
summary.zh: 普魯塔克筆下埃及祭司之優赫莫魯斯說：托特一手較短、塞特赤面、荷魯斯晳白、奧西里斯玄黑——皆同於凡人；奧西里斯乃將軍，卡諾普斯（星名）乃舵師——『希臘所謂阿爾戈號，乃仿奧西里斯之舟而造，因尊其人，化為星座，置於獵戶與天狼之側：前者屬荷魯斯，後者屬伊西斯。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient allegoresis via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: For when the Egyptians themselves tell us that Hermes had one hand shorter than another, that Typhon was of red complexion, Horus fair, and Osiris black, does not this show that they were of the human species, and subject to the same accidents as all other men? Nay, they go farther, and even declare the particular work in which each was engaged whilst alive.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XXII.

passages.text: Thus they say that Osiris was a general, that Canopus, from whom the star took its name, was a pilot, and that the ship which the Greeks call Argo, being made in imitation of the ship of Osiris, was, in honour of him, turned into a constellation and placed near Orion and the Dog-star, the former being sacred to Horus and the latter to Isis.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XXII.

title.en: No Women in the Temples: The Egyptian Rule of Purity
title.zh: 殿中無男女之事：埃及潔淨之律

region.en: Egyptian temples of all the gods

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.64 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 64

summary.en: The Egyptians, says Herodotus, were the first to make it a point of religion not to lie with women in temples, nor to enter a temple after going away from women without first bathing — while nearly all other men, 'since they hold that there is no difference in this respect between men and beasts', point to beasts coupling in the sacred enclosures as proof of divine consent; the Egyptians answer with Plato's dictum that none but the pure should approach the pure.
summary.zh: 希羅多德言：埃及人首立宗教之律——殿中不行男女之事，自婦人處來亦必先浴而後入廟——他邦之人則指聖域中獸之相配為神許之證，謂人獸無別；埃及人則守『唯淨者近於淨』之義。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnography via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Egyptians were the first who made it a point of religion not to lie with women in temples, nor to enter into temples after going away from women without first bathing: for almost all other men except the Egyptians and the Hellenes lie with women in temples and enter into a temple after going away from women without bathing, since they hold that there is no difference in this respect between men and beasts: for they say that they see beasts and the various kinds of birds coupling together both in the temples and in the sacred enclosures of the gods; if then this were not pleasing to the god, the beasts would not do so. Thus do these defend that which they do, which by me is disallowed: but the Egyptians are excessively careful in their observances, both in other matters which concern the sacred rites and also in those which follow.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.64. / Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.65.

title.en: The Goat of Mendes: Pan with the Goat's Face

region.en: Mendes, Nile Delta, Egypt (the sacred goat of the district)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲門德斯（其地聖羊）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.46 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 46

summary.en: The Mendesians count Pan among the eight elder gods, and the image-makers carve him with goat's face and legs 'not supposing him to be really like this but to resemble the other gods' — the reason for the form Herodotus declines to tell; they reverence all goats, the males above the females, goatherds above other herdsmen, and mourn greatly when their one sacred goat dies, for 'both the goat and Pan are called in the Egyptian tongue Mendes.'
summary.zh: 門德斯人列潘於八位先在之神；造像者刻其羊面羊足——『非謂其形實如此，乃擬他神之狀』——其形之故，希羅多德不欲言。彼等敬一切羊，雄踞雌上，牧羊人尊於他牧；其聖羊獨享尊榮，死則舉境大哀——蓋『羊與潘，埃及語皆名門德斯』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnographic myth via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Herodotus' final clause about the public marvel is reported without detail and is not quoted here.

passages.text: Now the reason why those of the Egyptians whom I have mentioned do not sacrifice goats, female or male, is this: — the Mendesians count Pan to be one of the eight gods (now these eight gods they say came into being before the twelve gods), and the painters and image-makers represent in painting and in sculpture the figure of Pan, just as the Hellenes do, with goat's face and legs, not supposing him to be really like this but to resemble the other gods; the cause however why they represent him in this form I prefer not to say.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.46.

passages.text: The Mendesians then reverence all goats and the males more than the females (and the goatherds too have greater honour than other herdsmen), but of the goats one especially is reverenced, and when he dies there is great mourning in all the Mendesian district: and both the goat and Pan are called in the Egyptian tongue Mendes.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.46.

title.en: Pigs of Dough: The Poor Man's Sacrifice to the Moon

region.en: Egypt, the full-moon sacrifice of the swine

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.47 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 47

summary.en: The pig is an abominable animal: whoever touches one dips in the river with his clothes on, swineherds may not enter temples or marry outside their caste — yet to the Moon and Dionysos alone, at the same full moon, swine are sacrificed and eaten; the priest burns the tail, spleen and caul in the fat, and 'the poor among them, by reason of the scantiness of their means, shape pigs of dough and having baked them they offer these as a sacrifice.'
summary.zh: 豕為可憎之獸：觸之者連衣入河自淨；牧豕者不得入廟、不得與他姓婚——然每月望日，唯月與狄俄倪索斯受豕祭而民得食之；祭司以脂裹尾、脾、網膜焚之——『其貧者因匱乏，乃摶麵為豕，炙而祭之。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual description via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Herodotus records that the mythic reason for the swine sacrifice is 'not a seemly one for me to tell'.

passages.text: The pig is accounted by the Egyptians an abominable animal; and first, if any of them in passing by touch a pig, he goes into the river and dips himself forthwith in the water together with his garments; and then too swineherds, though they be native Egyptians, unlike all others do not enter any of the temples in Egypt, nor is anyone willing to give his daughter in marriage to one of them or to take a wife from among them; but the swineherds both give in marriage to one another and take from one another.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.47.

passages.text: Now to the other gods the Egyptians do not think it right to sacrifice swine; but to the Moon and to Dionysos alone at the same time and on the same full-moon they sacrifice swine, and then eat their flesh: and as to the reason why, when they abominate swine at all their other feasts, they sacrifice them at this, there is a story told by the Egyptians; and this story I know, but it is not a seemly one for me to tell. — The poor however among them by reason of the scantiness of their means shape pigs of dough and having baked them they offer these as a sacrifice.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.47.
